content: Teleology, derived from the Greek word telos meaning end or purpose, is the philosophical study of design and purpose in the natural world. A teleological perspective asserts that all things are designed for or directed toward a final result, implying an inherent purpose or final cause for everything that exists. This view is traditionally contrasted with metaphysical naturalism, which denies the existence of design or purpose in nature. In teleology, form is defined by function, whereas in naturalism, function is defined by form. For example, teleology would argue that humans have eyes because they need eyesight (form follows function), while naturalism would claim that humans have eyesight simply because they have eyes (function follows form). In European philosophy, teleology is closely associated with Aristotelianism and the scholastic tradition. Many theological arguments, such as the concept of intelligent design, are inherently teleological, positing that the existence of God can be inferred from the purposeful design of the universe. Aristotle's analysis of causality includes material, efficient, and formal causes, all of which serve a final cause. Later, teleology became central to the speculative philosophy of Hegel and was explored in depth by Immanuel Kant in his Critique of Judgment. Teleology distinguishes between two types of final causes: intrinsic and extrinsic finality. Extrinsic finality refers to a being fulfilling a purpose outside itself, often for the benefit of other beings. For instance, minerals are designed to nourish plants, which in turn are designed to sustain animals, and humanity is thought to serve some ultimate good beyond itself. Intrinsic finality, on the other hand, involves a being realizing a purpose directed toward the perfection of its own nature, essentially what is good for that being. Just as physical masses obey universal gravitational tendencies, life is seen as inherently directed toward self-preservation and avoidance of death, disease, and pain. In bioethics, teleology is often used to describe the utilitarian view that the morality of an action is determined by its consequences, whether good or bad. Plato summarized the teleological position in his dialogue Phaedo, lamenting those who fail to distinguish between the ultimate cause and the means by which that cause acts. Similarly, Aristotle criticized Democritus, a proponent of atomic theory, for reducing all phenomena to mere necessity, neglecting the purpose, order, and final cause that underlie necessity. Both Plato and Aristotle agreed that lesser causes serve an ultimate good, while thinkers like Democritus and Lucretius supported metaphysical naturalism or accidentalism. In modern and postmodern philosophy, teleology has been interpreted and critiqued in various ways. Neo-Hegelian schools, for example, propose a history of humanity that is goal-driven, oriented toward an endpoint in history. Hegel conceived of the totality of conflicting worldviews and life forms in history as being directed toward a resolution, where the contradiction between subject and object would eventually sublate into a harmonious form of life, leaving violent conflict behind. This teleological notion of history as a whole has influenced 20th-century authors like Lukács, Jaspers, Horkheimer, and Adorno. However, postmodern attitudes often reject teleology and grand narratives, viewing them as reductive, exclusionary, and harmful to marginalized perspectives. In contrast, Alasdair MacIntyre has argued for a narrative understanding of oneself and social practices, suggesting that such practices are teleologically oriented toward internal goods, such as the pursuit of truth in philosophical and scientific inquiry. In science, teleology is often at odds with naturalistic explanations, as science focuses on physical causality and demonstrable mechanisms. However, teleological ideas persist in discussions about the origins and ultimate ends of phenomena. For example, in thermodynamics, the irreversibility of macroscopic processes has been described in teleological terms. In physics and cosmology, the anthropic principle, introduced by Brandon Carter in 1973, explores why the universe has evolved from a simple state (the Big Bang) to one that is not only hospitable to human life but also conducive to advanced human civilization. In chemistry, teleological arguments have historically centered on the suitability of materials to form the complex molecular bonds necessary for life. For instance, Lawrence Joseph Henderson, an American biochemist, advanced such views in the early 20th century. Biology has long been susceptible to teleological thought, even after Darwin proposed survival as the only observable final good. For example, Hans Driesch presented a modified vitalism in which an Aristotelian or Kantian entelechy drives embryonic development. Contemporary accounts of teleology in biology are heavily influenced by Larry Wright's etiological account, which defines function in a way applicable to both natural phenomena and human constructions, such as tools. Most contemporary accounts follow Wright's framework, though some, like Godfrey-Smith and Ernst Mayr, object to such theories, favoring naturalistic explanations of teleology. In cybernetics, feedback mechanisms have been interpreted as lending teleology to machinery. Norbert Wiener, a mathematician, coined the term cybernetics to describe the study of teleological mechanisms. Cybernetics examines the communication and control of regulatory feedback in living beings, machines, and their combinations, often referred to as teleonomy or process-driven systems. For a detailed discussion of the resurgence of teleology in natural science, one can refer to the work of Barrow and Tipler (1986). Their research includes a review of the intellectual history of teleology and design arguments, an exploration of teleological implications in earth science and chemistry (with reference to Henderson's work), a discussion of evolutionary biology's implications for teleology (highlighting the writings of Theodosius Dobzhansky and Ernst Mayr), and teleological speculations on the ultimate fate of the universe.
